ratings.reason: A particularly clean and unusual voice pipeline: natural speech is intercepted, rewritten into a legacy interface’s required syntax, and reinjected through virtual audio. The shim addresses a real compatibility breakdown and transfers broadly, although outcome impact cannot be confirmed from the abstract alone.

The quote clearly traces room speech through microphone capture and transcription to the Narrator agent. Voice enables hands-free, spatial participation, but speech-to-text feeding an agent is now a fairly established move; the distinctive contribution appears to be room-based storytelling rather than voice interaction itself.

The microphone-to-ASR-to-text control path is explicit, and hands-free operation is consequential for emergency responders. As evidence for this pattern, however, it shows a conventional transcription pipeline; the title suggests that the larger contribution is an evaluation framework rather than a new voice interaction mechanism.

Alexa converts the participant’s utterance into the text consumed by the therapy system, so the basic structural signature is present. Voice may materially improve access for people living with dementia, but the interaction shown is standard voice-assistant transcription and is tightly tied to this population and therapy setting.

Speech is the central authoring channel, enabling structured long-form composition while hands-free, eyes-free, and moving. That advances voice beyond short commands or literal dictation, though the supplied quote does not expose how the adaptive planning interaction actually works.
The quote only makes a general observation about how existing chart-authoring systems handle voice. It does not demonstrate that this paper built or specified an audio-entry control flow of its own.
ratings.disqualify_reason: The evidence quote does not support assignment of the paper's own interface to the Voice Interaction pattern.

ratings.reason: Users author interactive XR worlds through audio commands, making voice a consequential alternative to complex spatial authoring controls. Voice-to-world generation is useful, but the quote omits the conversion details, and much of the novelty likely resides in the LLM/JSON world-generation pipeline rather than the input modality.

A module performs speech-to-text and text-to-speech for robot communication, but voice appears to be infrastructure supporting the paper’s generative visual aids rather than its load-bearing design contribution. Bidirectional voice conversion is clear but highly conventional.

The user supplies email intent in one spoken turn, fitting an on-the-go wearable context and bypassing keyboard composition. The mechanism is legible, but single-turn voice prompting for email is a straightforward application of a settled interaction pattern.

Voice is explicitly the application’s only substantive input, although a controller button starts capture. Speaking is appropriate and potentially consequential for communication-skills rehearsal, but the voice mechanism itself is conventional and the design is specialized to VR training for autistic users.

Spoken words become generative material that transforms a photograph of the immediate environment. This is a crisp, non-obvious use of voice as creative control rather than mere transcription, although its broader practical impact and transferability cannot be established from the design-probe evidence alone.

NaviNote makes voice the hands-free control surface for querying space and creating, finding, editing, and deleting annotations. It addresses a genuine accessibility and mobility breakdown with a broad vocabulary of actions, and the spatial-annotation mechanism should transfer beyond this exact navigation system.

Speech acts convey actionable intent in an immersive analytics system, with context-aware clarification aimed at a central weakness of spoken commands. That is more substantive than adding transcription, though the quote remains conceptual and does not show the clarification exchange or downstream command representation.

The study uses Rambler to capture dictated thought segments, so speech clearly supplies writing material. This paper’s supplied evidence concerns a diary deployment of an already established interface, however, and shows neither a new voice mechanism nor enough outcome evidence to credit the pattern with strong impact here.

Three concrete speech commands replace controller-button remapping for accessible VR scene queries. The resulting accessibility benefit is plausible and the interaction is exceptionally reproducible, but a small fixed command vocabulary is a settled voice-interface design rather than a major expansion of the design space.

The application transcribes spoken responses, which is structurally appropriate for public-speaking rehearsal. The quote supplies only the ASR component, and voice is also inherent to the practiced task, so little distinctive voice-interface design can be credited from the available evidence.

VOICE accepts arbitrary spoken commands and replies verbally, making speech a broad control channel rather than a fixed vocabulary. Arbitrary-command scope is promising, but the quote does not explain command interpretation or supported actions, and conversational voice control is otherwise familiar.

The fragment confirms use of browser speech-to-text but establishes little about what utterances control or what the system consumes. Voice appears to be one implementation channel in a richer longitudinal storytelling project, with no visible voice-specific design move.

Wizundry is a meta-level platform for prototyping speech interfaces, including keyword detection and editing through natural speech. Supporting coordinated multi-wizard simulation is broadly reusable and unusual, but the supplied quote does not fully trace an actual audio-capture and conversion flow, so it is less clean as a direct exemplar.

Rambler substantially rethinks speech writing: users capture trains of thought, review them through generated semantic summaries, and revise at the conceptual rather than transcript level. The mechanism directly addresses the mismatch between linear speech and long-form composition and is both clearly specified and transferable.

The work explicitly introduces an LLM-integrated voice interface for surgical AR, where hands-free control could address a serious operational constraint. The quote does not reveal the commands, conversion pipeline, or observed outcomes, and the mechanism appears specialized to pancreatic-surgery assistance.

Conducting the interaction entirely by voice establishes modality but not the required capture-to-command pipeline. The interesting contribution suggested by the title is utterance re-presentation for self-awareness, not voice as an input design, so pattern-specific representativeness and impact are low.

Authors begin AR-instruction creation by speaking the intended content, making voice an authoring channel in a context where keyboard entry may be cumbersome. This is a meaningful workflow substitution, but the evidence does not show how speech becomes context-aware AR instructions or what editing remains necessary.

The system is voice-first, but explicitly multimodal, and the quote does not establish whether speech bypasses conventional controls or how it is transformed. Personalized cognitive training may be consequential, yet the novel contribution appears to be controllable LLM dialogue and reusable components rather than voice itself.

Users speak a request and explicitly submit it to an AR-building agent, so speech occupies the prompt slot even though interface controls remain involved. It is clear and reusable, but voice prompting an autonomous creation agent is a conventional substitution rather than the paper’s likely design advance.

A tangible microphone lets children create story content and converse with AI characters during embodied role-play. Coupling voice authoring to toy-mediated family drama is distinctive and developmentally appropriate, although the broader system has many other mechanisms and the quote does not expose the internal conversion pipeline.

A microphone button captures spoken scene-generation instructions, clearly placing voice in the request slot. This is a standard push-to-talk prompt affordance within a richer progressive VR design system, so the voice move itself contributes little novelty.

Users iteratively externalize speech into a node-link semantic canvas, directly tackling how nonlinear thought can emerge from a linear spoken stream. The combination is clear, broadly relevant to ideation and sensemaking, and more inventive than ordinary transcription, though outcome strength is not visible in the quote.

Microphone capture provides an appropriately hands-free conversational channel during automated driving, where reduced fatigue could matter. The quote does not describe transcription or actionable control flow, and spoken conversation is a predictable modality choice for a driver-attention intervention.

Visitors converse by speech with a life-sized exhibition agent, making voice a visible entry channel. The evidence shows no conversion or command mechanism, and spoken dialogue with an embodied public-facing agent is now a familiar installation pattern whose distinctive impact cannot be judged here.
